proposed_edges.relationship: In “Prejudice behind the pomp and baubles” (2001), MacKenzie argues that Cannadine’s Ornamentalism (2001) underweights racial hierarchies and capitalist interests by concentrating on elite rank and ceremonial display.
proposed_edges.map_label: Rank, race and the limits of ornamentalism, 2001
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete review body read on the journal’s own site. Exact unpaginated locators: paragraphs beginning “And this, perhaps”, “There are few testimonies”, “Were they as fascinated”, “Moreover, even if”, “Moreover, when we turn to the workers”, and “There were two imperial hierarchies”. MacKenzie questions the elite source base and stresses racial divisions among workers and economic power outside the honours system. His formulation is “There were two imperial hierarchies”. Closing paragraphs also praise Cannadine: the book “remains an important book”. This is a qualified published criticism, not wholesale rejection. Original review date 27 July 2001; the page’s 2015 update is not its publication year. Cannadine’s book itself remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: MacKenzie and T. M. Devine co-edited Scotland and the British Empire (2011) and co-authored its introduction, examining Scotland’s reciprocal relationships with empire.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Licensed publisher preview: title page names both editors; copyright page distinguishes first publication in 2011 from the 2016 paperback. Contents and introduction p. 1 identify both authors. Introduction pp. 1–6 read, especially p. 4 on metropolitan effects and relations among British ethnicities. Acknowledgements p. xv describe the volume as a “collaborative venture”. Contents also credit both for “Scots in the Imperial Economy”, p. 227 onward; that chapter is unread and no claim about its argument is proposed. Edinburgh’s institutional record independently confirms joint editorial credit and 2011. Undirected collaboration, not a claim that either scholar influenced the other.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hall, writing with Sonya Rose in “Introduction: being at home with the Empire” (2006), credits MacKenzie’s Studies in Imperialism with changing knowledge of metropolitan imperial culture and cites his argument linking empire to national identity and race-consciousness.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hall and Rose acknowledge metropolitan imperial history, 2006
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Licensed preview, printed pp. 12–13, nn. 46–47: the coauthors say the series “transformed our knowledge” and quote MacKenzie’s conclusion about national identity and race-consciousness, citing “Empire and Metropolitan Cultures” (1999), p. 292. Printed p. 17 further discusses a non-monolithic imperial culture. This is named, constructive scholarly reception in their joint historiographical argument; Rose’s coauthorship is essential, although she has no endpoint. It does not establish supervision, personal contact, or exclusive dependence. The original 1999 chapter remains unread. The introduction’s passing reference to an inaugural 1985 volume is not adopted: its own n. 46 gives Propaganda and Empire as 1984. Cambridge confirms print year 2006, distinct from online publication in 2011.

review.reviewer: Claude (independent verification agent; coordinator decisions by Claude)
review.phrase_seen: it has transformed our knowledge of many aspects of the Empire at home
review.reason: Hall and Rose, Introduction, printed pp. 12-13, nn. 46-47: the Studies in Imperialism series edited by MacKenzie 'transformed our knowledge'; they quote his OHBE conclusion that empire 'constituted a vital aspect of national identity and race-consciousness'; p. 17 'Like MacKenzie ... no single or monolithic imperial culture'. Print 2006. Supported as named reception in a historiographical survey; 'influence' is at the upper bound (reception, not a stated personal debt), as the evidence note concedes.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Empire and National Identities: The Case of Scotland” (1998), MacKenzie challenges Colley’s emphasis in Britons (1992) on British identity formed against France, arguing for greater attention to affirmative ethnic myths and positive referent societies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary journal PDF, printed pp. 217–218, nn. 8–12. MacKenzie names Colley’s oppositional account before arguing that “the binary Other has surely been emphasised too much”. This is a specific qualification of identity formation, not rejection of Britons as a whole. Colley’s book remains unread. Article published in 1998; delivered in 1997.

review.reviewer: Claude (independent verification agent; coordinator decisions by Claude)

review.reason: Read via Cambridge-hosted PDF of TRHS 6th ser. 8 (1998), pp. 217-218, nn. 8, 11. Read 26 September 1997, published 1998. Note: the criticism is aimed at 'many scholars ... including Linda Colley' (and Said and the postcolonialists), so Colley is a named target among several, not the sole one; the sentence is still accurate.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Empire and National Identities: The Case of Scotland” (1998), MacKenzie uses Anthony D. Smith’s National Identity (1991) to argue that national identities draw on myths of distinctive origins as well as contrasts with contemporary outsiders.
proposed_edges.map_label: Smith on ethnic myths and national identity, 1998
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary journal PDF, printed p. 218, n. 11: “as Anthony D. Smith has argued” introduces the account of uniqueness and historical depth, which MacKenzie develops into his alternative to negative identity construction. A specific argumentative resource; Smith’s 1991 book remains unread.
